summaries.headline: Detroit Parents Sue State Over District Funding Inequity
summaries.summary: A class-action lawsuit filed against Michigan seeks increased funding for Detroit Public Schools Community District and elimination of debt accumulated during state control of the system. The suit argues DPSCD's $10,050 per-student base funding falls short of what wealthier districts receive, with some allowed to spend significantly more due to provisions grandfathered in when the current system launched in the mid-1990s. The case echoes claims from a 2016 "right to read" lawsuit that resulted in a $94.4 million settlement, but now directly challenges the state's funding formula as constitutionally inadequate for Detroit students.

summaries.headline: States Launch New Curriculum Review and Literacy Initiatives
summaries.summary: Massachusetts's Department of Elementary and Secondary Education is seeking a facilitator to recruit and convene educator panels for reviewing the alignment and quality of core curricular materials across the state's nearly 900,000 students, with proposals due June 16. A Pennsylvania school system is simultaneously pursuing a literacy and family engagement program, while a Kentucky district searches for software to monitor instructional systems. These procurement moves signal states and districts are prioritizing systematic approaches to curriculum quality and family involvement as key levers for student outcomes.

summaries.headline: Detroit Lawsuit Seeks Equitable Funding as Transit Pilot Shows Mixed Results
summaries.summary: A Troy attorney filed a lawsuit against Michigan on behalf of a Detroit Public Schools Community District parent, seeking equitable funding for the district in a case that echoes the 2016 right-to-read lawsuit but focuses on financial resources rather than conditions. The district's yellow bus pilot program aimed at reducing chronic absenteeism succeeded at Henry Ford High School but failed at East English Village Preparatory Academy at Finney, with both schools receiving transportation services for select students. The split results highlight how targeted interventions can produce vastly different outcomes even within the same district, while the funding lawsuit signals continued legal pressure on state officials to address resource disparities in urban districts.

summaries.headline: Wake County Seeks SEL Curriculum for 161,000 Students
summaries.summary: Wake County Public School District, North Carolina's largest system, is seeking a web-based social-emotional learning curriculum for grades K-8 to support its counseling and student services department. The district requires research-backed materials that address bullying prevention and student well-being, with potential for future expansion to high school grades. The move signals how large districts are formalizing SEL programming through dedicated curriculum purchases rather than piecemeal approaches.

summaries.headline: Detroit Bus Pilot Cuts Chronic Absenteeism at Henry Ford
summaries.summary: Detroit Public Schools Community District's $600,000 yellow bus pilot at two high schools produced mixed results, with Henry Ford High School seeing reduced chronic absenteeism among frequent riders while East English Village Preparatory Academy showed inconclusive outcomes due to low participation. Henry Ford attracted 102 student riders compared to just 29 at East English Village, where fewer students live within the school's feeder pattern, limiting eligibility for the transportation service. The contrasting results suggest that yellow bus service works best for neighborhood schools with concentrated nearby populations, potentially informing the district's future transportation investments as it weighs expansion against a backdrop of district-wide chronic absenteeism rates above 60 percent.

summaries.headline: Screen Time Fears Fuel EdTech Vetting Backlash
summaries.summary: Legislators are pushing new scrutiny on educational software following broader concerns about student screen time and device usage in schools. The backlash extends beyond cellphone restrictions to target the processes districts use to evaluate and approve educational technology tools. Districts now face increased pressure to justify their technology choices amid growing skepticism about digital learning tools that parents and policymakers once embraced during remote learning.

summaries.headline: LAUSD Board Member Proposes Coordinated Mental Health Approach
summaries.summary: Los Angeles Unified board member Karla Griego introduced a resolution last month to expand student mental health support beyond individual counselors through coordinated staff efforts. The proposal includes creating a trauma index to strategically deploy mental health workers based on student needs and establishing professional development to help educators respond to wellness challenges. Griego's initiative comes as LAUSD communities face heightened stress from immigration enforcement and economic pressures, suggesting districts may need systematic approaches rather than crisis-driven responses to address mounting student mental health demands.

summaries.headline: Newark Leaders Target Reading Crisis as Half Struggle
summaries.summary: New Jersey education leaders are mobilizing to address literacy challenges after test scores show roughly half of state students cannot read on grade level. Last spring, only 34% of Newark Public Schools students in grades 3-9 passed the state's English Language Arts test, while statewide 53% of students met proficiency standards. Teach for America New Jersey is convening local stakeholders to develop targeted solutions, recognizing that reading deficits follow students into adulthood with limited options for remediation.

summaries.headline: NYC Schools Lack Data Privacy Oversight Despite AI Push
summaries.summary: A state audit found New York City public schools "does not have a clear understanding" of student data it collects or security risks it faces, citing major gaps in required data policies and multiple breaches involving third-party software used across the 900,000-student system. The five-year review spanning 2020 to 2025 revealed the district lacks a complete inventory of school software and has weaknesses in tracking and securing student information, though auditors found no direct federal privacy law violations. The findings surface as NYC rolls out its new AI framework that could significantly expand technology use in classrooms from lesson planning to translation services.

summaries.headline: Academic Launches Audio App for Workplace AI Literacy
summaries.summary: Marcel Salathe, co-director of EPFL's AI Center, is launching The Framework, a subscription audio app designed to teach professionals how to think about AI rather than use specific tools. The app features 50 sequential lessons based on his previously German and French-only book, plus ongoing shorter explorations on emerging developments, priced at £15 monthly or £99 annually for its May 2026 launch. The approach reflects growing demand for AI literacy content aimed at working professionals rather than technical students, positioning audio learning as a way to build durable understanding during daily activities.

summaries.headline: NYC Parents Demand AI Moratorium in Marathon Board Meeting
summaries.summary: More than 100 New York City parents, students, and educators testified at a nearly seven-hour school board meeting demanding greater transparency and restrictions on artificial intelligence use in schools, despite the controversial AI-focused high school proposal being pulled from the agenda. Community members argued the Education Department is deploying AI tools without clear rules or adequate understanding, pointing to existing surveillance technologies like digital bathroom hall passes already operating in 150 city schools that conflict with the district's preliminary AI policy released in March. The sustained public pressure signals growing parental resistance to educational technology adoption in the nation's largest school system, where AI integration is advancing faster than governance frameworks.

summaries.headline: White Families Dominate NYC Special Education Private Tuition
summaries.summary: New York City spent $723 million last school year paying private school tuition for students with disabilities, with nearly 71% of those payments going to white families who represent just 12.5% of the district's students with disabilities. Black and Latino children, who make up about 75% of students with disabilities, received only 24% of tuition reimbursements through the legal process that allows families to prove the public system cannot adequately serve their children. The 300% spending increase over the past decade and stark racial disparities in who accesses these funds arrive as Mayor Mamdani faces pressure to close a multi-billion dollar budget gap.

summaries.headline: Chicago Schools Face Inevitable Budget Cuts Despite Lobbying
summaries.summary: Chicago Public Schools is preparing to release campus budgets next week that will likely include cuts to its roughly 500 schools, as the district grapples with a projected deficit of about $700 million. CEO Macquline King has warned of a worst-case scenario reaching $1 billion, forcing potential reductions to positions like bilingual coordinators and counselors after years of budget stability bolstered by now-expired federal COVID relief funds. The looming cuts come as state lawmakers question the district's thousands of recent hires despite continued enrollment declines, signaling limited appetite for additional state funding even as CPS remains $1.6 billion below Illinois's adequacy threshold.

summaries.headline: Federal School Data Updates Stop After Research Cuts
summaries.summary: The Education Department has stopped updating core statistical information about American schools since the Trump administration eliminated the research arm that compiled the Digest of Education Statistics. Key data tables on per-pupil spending, federal funding, enrollment trends, and special education services have not been refreshed since at least January 2025, leaving district leaders without current benchmarks for decision-making. The department says it will award a new contract by September to restart the work, but the gap means shared knowledge about school operations continues to deteriorate as leaders navigate budget cycles and policy decisions with increasingly stale information.

summaries.headline: Travel Website Misreports Higher Ed AI Conference
summaries.summary: A travel industry publication incorrectly categorized a higher education conference presentation about AI assessment tools as K-12 education news. The American College of Healthcare Sciences demonstrated AI-resistant assessment methods at a Western Senior College and University Commission conference, focusing on workforce-aligned credentials for adult learners. The misplaced coverage highlights how AI and assessment innovations in higher education often get conflated with K-12 concerns, despite serving entirely different student populations and institutional needs.

summaries.headline: Reading Intervention Boosts Math Scores Through Transfer
summaries.summary: A follow-up study of Harvard's Model of Reading Engagement found that literacy instruction can improve math performance through learning transfer, with students who made greater reading gains in third grade scoring higher on fourth-grade math tests. The intervention, which integrates reading with science and social studies content, produced math improvements even though it contained no explicit math instruction—researchers tracked 2,073 students across 30 schools to isolate the specific mechanisms behind these cross-curricular gains. The findings suggest that content-rich literacy programs may offer districts a pathway to address multiple academic areas simultaneously, particularly as schools search for interventions that maximize limited instructional time.

summaries.headline: Canvas Breach Exposes 275 Million User Records
summaries.summary: The ShinyHunters hacking group breached Instructure's Canvas learning management system in early May, stealing personal data from 275 million users across nearly 9,000 schools worldwide. The compromised information includes names, email addresses, student IDs, and billions of private messages between students, teachers, and staff, though Instructure says passwords were not accessed. The scale of exposure—affecting one of education's most widely used platforms—underscores how deeply embedded edtech systems have become in daily school operations and communication.

summaries.headline: Queensland Schools Hit by Global Data Breach
summaries.summary: Queensland schools experienced a significant data breach through their QLearn educational platform, exposing student and staff information to unauthorized access. The incident appears to be part of a broader cybersecurity attack affecting educational technology systems globally, though specific details about the number of schools or individuals affected remain unclear from available reports. School districts relying on centralized learning management systems now face heightened scrutiny over their data protection protocols and vendor security standards.

summaries.headline: Districts Deploy Home Visits, Teams to Fight Absenteeism
summaries.summary: Syracuse City School District launched a $2 million "Rise and Thrive" initiative that stations attendance teams at every school to conduct home visits, make phone calls, and meet with parents after reporting a 43% chronic absenteeism rate in 2025. The district says 83% of schools have seen attendance increases since implementing the program, while nearby Liverpool High School faces a 29% chronic absenteeism rate affecting more than 580 students. The targeted outreach approach signals districts are treating attendance as requiring the same systematic intervention as academic struggles, moving beyond traditional office-based responses to meet families where they are.

summaries.headline: Justice Department Probes 36 Illinois Districts on LGBTQ Content
summaries.summary: The Justice Department has launched investigations into 36 Illinois school districts to examine whether they include LGBTQ+-inclusive content in classrooms and whether they provide parental opt-out options for such materials. The federal agency did not specify which districts are under investigation or provide details about the scope of the probes. The investigations signal a significant federal intervention in local curriculum decisions and could establish precedents for how districts nationwide navigate the intersection of inclusive education policies and parental rights demands.

synthesis.topic_title: Literacy Gains Momentum: Districts Expand Digital Tools and Financial Education
synthesis.whats_happening: School districts are broadening their literacy focus beyond traditional reading instruction, integrating digital platforms for engagement tracking and adding financial literacy components. Recognition programs are highlighting successful literacy initiatives as districts work to sustain momentum from recent improvements.
synthesis.whats_driving: The expansion reflects districts' growing understanding that modern literacy encompasses both digital fluency and practical life skills like financial education. Post-pandemic emphasis on measurable outcomes is driving districts to adopt technology platforms that provide clear engagement data while addressing learning gaps across diverse student populations.

# Student Reading App Sora Reports on Digital Literacy Trends

By Nathalie op de Beeck

\|



May 05, 2026


![](https://www.publishersweekly.com/loading.gif)

Audio Native

Listen to This Article

00:00

03:36

1.0x

[\|\|ElevenLabs](https://elevenlabs.io/?utm_medium=audionative&utm_source=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.publishersweekly.com%2Fpw%2Fby-topic%2Findustry-news%2Flibraries%2Farticle%2F100326-student-reading-app-sora-reports-on-digital-literacy-trends.html&utm_campaign=audionative_www.publishersweekly.com&utm_term=creator_public_id_81a124bca97e51d9f8d64cf4076617209c536192d26bc409a4172a6d3defc042&utm_content=project_id_w4wNAyiRvKuX08BONSTE)

Sora, OverDrive’s student reading platform, has released its [third annual report](https://www.discoversora.com/2025-state-of-reading-report) on K–12 digital reading and borrowing trends. The report covers data collected during the 2024–2025 school year, when more than four million students completed nearly 60 million digital checkouts. Of the checkouts, 85% were e-books, 11% were audiobooks, and 4% were magazines, and the top five states checking out e-books—in order—were Texas, New York, California, Massachusetts, and Wisconsin.

Using anonymized data to maintain student privacy, Sora’s team charted how long an average student spent reading on the platform per month and how frequently readers accessed features such as the dictionary and annotation. As of March 2026, more than 628,000 students had set reading goals and “most commonly chose 20 minutes per day” as their goal, Sora reported.

Molly Ness, founder and CEO of literacy consulting firm Dirigo Literacy, writes in an introduction that educational “screens are not created equal,” and points to Sora’s “adaptive features, its ability to monitor students’ reading frequency and duration, and its diverse content.” To increase engagement, the app awards badges for milestones such as finishing borrowed books, and in 2024, it introduced a setting that informs students how long they’ve spent reading.

“Sustained reading habits are critical to student success and understanding how students actually engage with text is essential for educators,” Sora VP of education Renee Davenport wrote in a statement. “This report offers a clear, data-informed picture of how digital reading is supporting instruction, choice, and access at a time when literacy outcomes are under increasing scrutiny.”

Because students use Sora for assigned and leisure reading, the data show a blend of library materials and tastes. Seven of Sora’s top 10 elementary- and middle-school e-book checkouts in 2024–2025 were from Jeff Kinney’s Wimpy Kid series, while the top young adult checkouts included Lois Lowry’s _The Giver_, Suzanne Collins’s _The Hunger Games_, Alice Oseman’s Heartstopper books one and two, and Twisted Ones titles by Scott Cawthon. E-books categorized as “adult” but borrowed by students included course content— _To Kill a Mockingbird_, _Fahrenheit 451_, _Animal Farm_—side by side with licensed content on Super Mario, Roblox, and Sonic the Hedgehog.

In addition, from the 2023–2024 to 2024–2025 school years, Sora researchers found an 11% increase in lending of books in languages other than English. K–8 students read e-book editions of Raina Telgemeier’s _Courage_ in French and Dav Pilkey’s Dog Man books in Spanish, and older readers read a Spanish version of Marissa Meyer’s _Cinder_. Popular audiobooks for younger students included a Spanish-language edition of Peter Brown’s _The Wild Robot_, while older readers borrowed Spanish audiobook versions of George Orwell's _1984_ and Andy Weir’s _Project Hail Mary_.

In the report, Sora’s team wrote that multilingual learners “can read privately and explore content suited to their reading level and interests,” indicating the educational and social value of dual-language library offerings.

![Luann Zant named recipient of the 2026 National 180 Awards](https://core-docs.s3.amazonaws.com/okaloosa_county_school_district_ar/article/image/large_dc3ddb76-b819-4ef2-af6d-e5d170138444.jpeg)

## Okaloosa County School District Celebrates National Recognition for Outstanding Literacy Achievement

OCSD Webmaster

May 6, 2026

The Okaloosa County School District is proud to announce that a dedicated educator has been selected as a recipient of the 2026 National 180 Awards, a prestigious national recognition celebrating outstanding achievement in literacy and academic growth. Luann Zant, an Intensive Reading teacher at Pryor Middle School, has been honored with the 180 Educator Award for her unwavering commitment to student success, mentorship, and her ability to help students achieve significant academic milestones. This national recognition highlights her exceptional impact in the classroom and her dedication to fostering both literacy skills and student confidence.

Educators recognized through the National 180 Awards are selected based on teaching excellence, measurable student growth, innovative instructional practices, including whole-group and small-group rotational models, student engagement through application use, and alignment with the program’s core values. Mrs. Zant was nominated by her colleague, Donna Born, with whom she works closely.

“Mrs. Zant represents the very best of Okaloosa County School District,” said Superintendent Marcus Chambers. “Her passion for literacy and her commitment to ensuring every student succeeds reflect the heart of our mission. While I could not attend the recognition in person, I could not be prouder of the incredible work she is doing to change the trajectory of students’ lives through reading. This honor is well deserved and a testament to her impact both inside and beyond the classroom.”

Pryor Middle School Principal Jason McClelland praised Mrs. Zant’s dedication and instructional excellence. “Mrs. Zant is deeply committed to the success of every student in her Intensive Reading class,” said McClelland. “She knows exactly how to challenge and support students, pushing them just enough to help them grow in confidence and achievement. When you step into her classroom, you immediately see engaging, interactive lessons and students who are actively involved in learning. Pryor Middle School is truly fortunate to have Mrs. Zant. She consistently goes above and beyond to ensure her students are supported, motivated, and successful. We are so proud of Mrs. Zant, Pirate Pride!”

Mrs. Zant, who has been teaching at Pryor Middle School for nearly 11 years, shared her passion for literacy and student growth. “I am passionate about helping middle school students develop strong reading skills that will serve them for a lifetime, while also fostering a love of reading,” said Zant. “One of the most rewarding parts of my job is witnessing those ‘lightbulb’ moments, when everything finally clicks and students gain confidence in themselves as readers. Those moments are what continue to inspire me.”

Elease McDonald, District Curriculum Specialist for the Okaloosa County School District, emphasized the lasting impact of reading educators. “Few occupations are more noble or more rewarding than being a reading teacher,” said McDonald. “You open doors to the world that students will walk through for the rest of their lives. Literacy is the foundation of everything, and we are incredibly fortunate to have teachers as dedicated to that mission as Mrs. Zant.”

The Okaloosa County School District congratulates Mrs. Zant on this outstanding national recognition and celebrates the continued commitment of its educators to student success and academic excellence.

**By FATIMA HUSSEIN**

WASHINGTON (AP) — [Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent](https://apnews.com/hub/us-department-of-the-treasury) winces at the allure of easy money — whether it’s lottery tickets, [buy now, pay later loans](https://apnews.com/article/buy-now-pay-later-loans-installments-02852578a991fb0d31879acd0b687e0d) or the promise of a crypto windfall — warning that the get-rich-quick mindset often leads Americans farther from financial stability, not closer to it.

“There are a lot of young people, mostly young men, going to blue-collar construction jobs, playing the lottery. It drives me crazy,” Bessent said in an interview.

”The best thing you can do is not play the lottery,” he said — rather, people should invest and “then watch it grow.”

Bessent spoke to The Associated Press about the basics of building a workable budget and saving for the future at the tail end of Financial Literacy Month, an initiative the billionaire hedge fund manager has made a priority since joining President Donald Trump’s administration, driven by a childhood marred by poverty.

Former Treasury Secretaries Hank Paulson and Tim Geithner were known for helping navigate the U.S. out of the global financial crisis. [Steven Mnuchin](https://apnews.com/hub/steven-mnuchin) made his mark designing and promoting the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, and [Janet Yellen](https://apnews.com/hub/janet-yellen) was the only person to also head the Federal Reserve and the Council of Economic Advisers. But Bessent’s passion for meeting with community bankers, retirees and schoolchildren to talk about how to budget, save and manage debt is what he hopes, in part, defines his legacy.

His push to promote financial literacy comes as Americans grapple with the cost of housing, groceries, energy and everyday items and are skeptical about the Republican administration’s performance on the issue. [The latest AP-NORC poll data](https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/trumps-approval-on-economy-falls-in-ap-norc-poll-showing-new-warning-signs-for-president-2/) shows Trump’s approval rating on the economy dropped from 38% in March to 30% in April.

The nation is enmeshed in record levels of debt, which [surpassed $39 trillion in March](https://apnews.com/article/us-national-deficit-hits-39-million-6ff73495bae701b5c009d3da5515ca3a), and critics wonder how Bessent can persuade Americans to save for their futures when [the government itself is drowning in debt](https://apnews.com/hub/national-debt).

“The Trump administration in particular has a problematic record on cutting taxes without offsets and growing spending,” said Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget.

![Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent attends a meeting](https://www.bostonherald.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Bessent_Profile_79393.jpg)

#### A billionaire with humble beginnings

Bessent, 63, made his money through a long career in hedge funds, including working with [George Soros](https://apnews.com/hub/george-soros), a financier and philanthropist whom [Trump and other Republicans have vilified](https://apnews.com/article/trump-indictment-soros-conspiracy-9dc8a81d35421388d82be25600db53f8). Bessent was famously involved in the Soros firm’s 1992 currency speculation against the British pound tied to Black Wednesday, which generated massive profits. Bessent later launched his own hedge fund called the Key Square Group.

But he often talks about his humble beginnings in rural South Carolina, not far from Myrtle Beach, where at the age of 9 he got his first jobs as a busboy at a cafeteria and hustling to set up chairs and umbrellas on the beach. His father, a real estate developer, had lost generations of Bessent family wealth by overleveraging his obligations.

Bessent wanted to attend the U.S. Naval Academy in 1979 but was barred as an openly gay applicant. That also shut the door to joining the foreign service.

He went to Yale University, where his former professor David Darst recalled teaching him about new financial instruments in capital markets. Darst described Bessent as a “guy who’s working at the highest levels, but he’s interested in people learning the ABCs of finance.”

In 2025, Bessent became the nation’s first openly gay treasury secretary. “I sit here knowing that President Trump chose me because he believes I’m the best candidate, not because of my sexual preference, not because treasury secretaries with green eyes do better,” Bessent said at [his confirmation hearing](https://apnews.com/article/bessent-trump-inauguration-treasury-finance-0da57f77f3a2010744cb157dd3d976a4).

After reaching public office, one of Bessent’s first actions was relaunching Financial Literacy Month at the agency.

“Wall Street has grown wealthier than ever before, and it can continue to grow and do well,” Bessent has peppered into various speeches over the past year, insisting that his work in the Trump administration is “focused on Main Street.”

During a roundtable with community financial institutions at the department — one of several such events Bessent hosted last month — he listened to bankers express concerns about the a surge in sophisticated fraud schemes targeting customers and their efforts to get high schoolers interested in saving.

“It could be as simple as a 14-year-old starting a savings account and watching interest compound at 4% a year,” said Thomas Fraser, CEO of First Mutual Holding Co. in Lakewood, Ohio, who attended that roundtable.

#### Promoting financial literacy to young people

Bessent is not a newcomer to preaching financial literacy. Geoff Canada, president of Harlem Children’s Zone, has known Bessent for 30 years and said the treasury secretary has mentored one of the program’s scholars for more than a decade. Canada said Bessent has a “deep understanding that financial literacy is essential for fostering real social and economic mobility for America’s children.”

He said Bessent “has championed this issue long before joining the administration, and I know it remains a top priority.”

A conversation with Bessent about financial literacy inevitably turns to [Trump Accounts](https://apnews.com/article/trump-accounts-kids-michael-dell-1831095c23ead75b67edc65ead5309fd) — the financial vehicle meant to give $1,000 to babies born during the Trump administration. That money is then invested in the stock market by private firms, and the [children can access the money](https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/spotlights/2026/your-baby-could-qualify-for-1000-with-a-trump-account-heres-what-to-know/) when they turn 18.

Bessent said he thinks it will encourage a generation of young people to care more about investing as it shows them “the power of compounding, because that money is locked up for 18 years.”

But Bessent said people of all ages and income brackets could be better at managing their money. “There’s a narrative that doctors are famously terrible at finance,” Bessent said.

Critics of the treasury secretary’s approach argue that the problem is less about Americans not knowing how to invest and more about people not having enough spare income to do so, as [the cost of living](https://apnews.com/article/inflation-prices-gas-federal-reserve-trump-bf00c3105d5da88a0b01d9107ed4ecee) has steadily increased and [the war in Iran](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DbawETUtQgc) has driven energy prices higher.

“You cannot preach penny-pinching while making it harder for Americans to pay their grocery, utility and healthcare bills,” said Emily DiVito, senior adviser for economic policy at the left-leaning Groundwork Collaborative. “If Secretary Bessent is serious about advancing financial literacy, he should focus on lowering the cost of living for working families.”

#### Rising debt in the foreground

Bessent’s desire to see Americans invest wisely comes as the U.S. debt has reached record levels — and the trajectory of those increases is a cause for concern for budgeting experts.

The U.S. national debt hit [$37 trillion](https://apnews.com/article/treasury-debt-spending-trump-obbb-6f807c4aae78dcc96f29ff07a3c926f4) in August and then [$38 trillion](https://apnews.com/article/trump-treasury-debt-ceiling-bessent-09575f13ca95c2f1beb38234b2cbe85b) just two months later. Now, it’s at [$39 trillion](https://apnews.com/article/us-national-deficit-hits-39-million-6ff73495bae701b5c009d3da5515ca3a) and has surpassed the size of the economy.

Budget advocate MacGuineas warned that the long-term trend of borrowing more and paying more in interest will force Americans to face tougher fiscal tradeoffs ahead.

She praised Bessent for having the goal to cut deficits in half and bring them down to 3% of gross domestic product but said ”it’s going to take a combination of spending reductions, revenue increases and economic growth” to get there.

The Treasury argues that the federal deficit decreased during Trump’s first year back in office and that the provisions in [Republicans’ tax cuts law](https://apnews.com/article/what-is-republican-trump-tax-bill-f65be44e1050431a601320197322551b) have put money back in Americans’ pockets.

“It’s hard to disagree with the fact that we need more financial literacy in this country,” MacGuineas said. “The bigger picture, of course, is that we should also probably give a financial literacy class to our lawmakers.”

Midland Public Schools is celebrating its students and educators recognized by the Rotary Club of Midland Morning at its eighth Claire's Day celebration, an event that celebrates students and teachers in Midland County who are making strides to improve literacy and walking the path to become or encourage lifelong readers.

![](https://cdn-channels-pixel.ex.co/events/0012000001fxZm9AAE?integrationType=DEFAULT&template=design%2Farticle%2Fplatypus_two_column.tpl)

Elementary teachers were invited to select second-grade students who demonstrated significant improvement in their reading skills over the course of the school year to receive a Claire’s Award for Reading Excellence (C.A.R.E.). These awards honor K–8 students who demonstrate significant improvement in reading skills, often overcoming learning challenges. Student winners received a certificate, a book and an ice cream coupon.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

MPS C.A.R.E recipients are:

- Emmadelle Downing, Central Park Elementary
- Ronin Freeman, Chestnut Hill Elementary
- Daniel Goff, Central Park Elementary
- Hailey Lemon, Woodcrest Elementary
- Niko Nielsen, Chestnut Hill Elementary
- Addison Rau, Adams Elementary
- Zoey Rousseau, Adams Elementary
- Raelynn Schaeding, Central Park Elementary
- Vivian Warmbier, Plymouth Elementary
- Caroline Wickstrom, Adams Elementary
- Ryder Wirtz, Central Park Elementary
- Finnegan Wymbs, Chestnut Hill Elementary

In addition to students, the Club also honored elementary school teachers with the Inspirational Teacher Award. This award was given to educators nominated by their principals for inspiring students to improve their reading skills and encouraging a passion for reading. Adams Elementary kindergarten teacher Amy Richard and Central Park Elementary first-grade teacher Rebecca Stern were recognized with the Inspirational Teacher Award.

“Early literacy is a top priority at Midland Public Schools, and we are intentional about building strong reading skills from the very beginning of a child’s educational journey,” Superintendent Penny Miller-Nelson said. “The growth these students have shown reflects their hard work and the consistent, thoughtful efforts of our elementary teachers. We are incredibly proud of both our students and staff for receiving these recognitions, and we look forward to continuing to watch these students grow and succeed.”

# Volunteers sought to teach financial literacy

Thursday, May 07, 2026 12:05 am

![](https://www.hawaiitribune-herald.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/05/web1_David-Earles.jpg)

EARLES

[Share by Email](mailto:?subject=Volunteers%20sought%20to%20teach%20financial%20literacy&body=https://www.hawaiitribune-herald.com/2026/05/07/community/volunteers-sought-to-teach-financial-literacy/ "Share by Email")

Share this story

While Financial Literacy Month in Hawaii has come to an end in April, there are still opportunities this school year for volunteers to get involved and help teach Junior Achievement of Hawaii’s (JAH) award-winning financial literacy and entrepreneurship curriculum to students in kindergarten through 12th-grade classrooms across the state.

“Last year, we had more than 200 volunteers in classrooms reaching more than 8,300 students in 372 kindergarten through 12th-grade classes and after-school locations on Oahu, Hawaii Island and Maui,” David Earles, JAH president, said in a press release. “Our supporters tell us time and time again that connecting with these students through our interactive programming is one of the most rewarding experiences they have had.”

##### ADVERTISING

* * *

Volunteering is fun and easy with JAH providing a one-hour training and all the materials needed to be successful in the classroom for five 45-minute in-person sessions.

While volunteers are needed year-round each school year, the most urgent needs before the close of this school year are on Hawaii Island with the following schools:

— Waiakea Elementary: Two 4th-grade classes. Mondays and Fridays in May. Flexible times between 12:05 p.m. to 2:05 p.m.

— Keaau Elementary: Six 3rd-grade classes. Six volunteers needed for May. Flexible dates and times.

— Kaumana Elementary: Two kindergarten classes. Back-to-back classes on Thursdays in May from 12:15 p.m. to 1 p.m. and 1 p.m. to 1:45 p.m. Two volunteers (one for each class) or one volunteer who can teach both classes.

To volunteer, visit hawaii.ja.org/volunteer/index or call JAH at (808) 286-5376.
